questions.question: In pharmacology, a drug that activates a receptor to produce an effect similar to the physiological signal molecule is called a/an:
questions.explanation: An agonist activates a receptor to produce an effect similar to that of the natural (physiological) signal molecule. An antagonist, by contrast, prevents an agonist's action without producing an effect of its own.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: A 'partial agonist' is best described as a drug that:

options.A: Blocks a receptor completely with no effect of its own
options.B: Activates a receptor to produce a submaximal effect, and can also antagonize a full agonist
options.C: Produces an effect opposite to that of the natural agonist
options.D: Binds only to enzymes, never to receptors

questions.explanation: A partial agonist has affinity for the receptor and submaximal intrinsic activity (between 0 and 1) — it produces a weaker effect than a full agonist, and because it occupies the receptor, it can also blunt (antagonize) the effect of a full agonist present at the same time.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: Which class of receptors produces the fastest onset of response, typically within milliseconds?
questions.explanation: Ligand-gated ion channel receptors (e.g. nicotinic cholinergic, GABA-A) have the ion channel built directly into the receptor molecule, so agonist binding opens the channel immediately with no intermediate second messenger — giving the fastest response of all receptor types, in milliseconds.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: The structural hallmark of a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) is:

options.A: A single transmembrane helix linked to an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain
options.B: Seven membrane-spanning helical segments with the agonist binding site on the extracellular face
options.C: A pentameric ring of subunits directly enclosing an ion channel
options.D: A soluble intracellular protein that binds directly to DNA

questions.explanation: GPCRs share a common structural motif: 7 alpha-helical membrane-spanning segments forming 3 extracellular and 3 intracellular loops, with the agonist binding site located between the helices on the extracellular face and the G-protein binding site on the cytosolic side.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: Activation of a Gi-coupled receptor typically has which effect on adenylyl cyclase and cAMP?

options.C: Has no effect on adenylyl cyclase, acts only on phospholipase C

questions.explanation: Gi (inhibitory G-protein) inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering intracellular cAMP — the opposite of Gs, which activates adenylyl cyclase and raises cAMP. This is why, for example, muscarinic M2 receptor stimulation (Gi-coupled) in the heart opposes the effect of beta-adrenergic (Gs-coupled) stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: In the two-state receptor model (Ra = active, Ri = inactive conformation), an inverse agonist is one that:

options.A: Binds Ra and Ri with exactly equal affinity, producing no net change
options.B: Has high affinity for the Ri (inactive) state, shifting equilibrium away from Ra and producing an effect opposite to the agonist
options.C: Cannot bind the receptor at all in either state
options.D: Only functions on receptors with no baseline (constitutive) activity

questions.explanation: An inverse agonist preferentially binds and stabilizes the inactive (Ri) receptor conformation. This only produces an observable opposite effect on receptors that show constitutive activation (some baseline Ra signal even without agonist) — by pulling the equilibrium further toward Ri, it reduces signalling below the unstimulated baseline.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: Allopurinol reduces uric acid production by acting as a competitive inhibitor of which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Allopurinol competitively inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that converts hypoxanthine to uric acid, which is why it is used to lower uric acid levels (e.g. in gout).
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: A drug that reacts with an enzyme's catalytic site so strongly (via a covalent bond or very high affinity) that the normal substrate cannot displace it produces which kinetic pattern?

options.A: kM unchanged, Vmax unchanged (no real inhibition)
options.C: kM increased and Vmax reduced — a non-equilibrium type of competitive inhibition
options.D: Only Vmax changes while kM decreases proportionally

questions.explanation: Classical competitive inhibition (equilibrium type) raises kM but leaves Vmax unchanged, since enough substrate can still out-compete the inhibitor. But when the inhibitor binds essentially irreversibly at the same catalytic site (e.g. organophosphates on cholinesterase, or methotrexate's very high affinity for dihydrofolate reductase), substrate can no longer displace it — this non-equilibrium type raises kM AND reduces Vmax.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: The existence of 'spare receptors' (receptor reserve) explains which observed phenomenon?

options.A: Some full agonists can produce a maximal response while occupying less than 1% of available receptors
options.B: All antagonists eventually become agonists at high enough doses
options.C: Receptor numbers never change regardless of chronic drug exposure
options.D: Enzymes and receptors are functionally identical structures

questions.explanation: When a tissue has a large receptor reserve, a full agonist can produce its maximal biological response by occupying only a small fraction of the total available receptors — occupying more receptors beyond that doesn't increase the effect further, since the response has already plateaued.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: Insulin and epidermal growth factor (EGF) act through which type of receptor?
questions.explanation: Insulin, EGF, and many other growth factors act through receptor tyrosine kinases: hormone binding causes receptor dimerization, activating an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain that autophosphorylates and triggers downstream signalling — a process that plays out over minutes to hours, much slower than ion-channel receptors.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: Glucocorticoid receptors are unique among the major receptor families in that they:

options.A: Are located on the cell surface and open ion channels directly
options.B: Are intracellular soluble proteins that, once liganded, dimerize and bind DNA to regulate gene transcription
options.D: Have no known endogenous ligand (are 'orphan receptors')

questions.explanation: Glucocorticoid receptors sit in the cytoplasm bound to HSP-90 and other inhibitory proteins. When the lipid-soluble steroid penetrates the cell and binds the receptor, HSP-90 is released, the receptor dimerizes, and the complex moves to the nucleus to bind glucocorticoid-responsive elements (GREs) on DNA, altering gene transcription — a fundamentally different, much slower mechanism than membrane receptors.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: A binding site that attaches a drug but produces no pharmacological response at all (e.g. many plasma protein binding sites) is best termed a:

options.B: Silent receptor (or drug acceptor / site of loss)

questions.explanation: Sites that bind a drug without producing any response are called silent receptors, or more accurately drug acceptors / sites of loss — the term 'receptor' is best reserved for binding sites capable of generating an actual biological response.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
